entries.title: 'Like gods reigning over humans': Many defectors see daughter of North Korea's Kim as heir apparent
entries.summary: Little is known about her except that she's reportedly about 13 and named Kim Ju Ae, but Korea's spy agency says she's likely her father's heir.
entries.content:
'Like gods reigning over humans': Many defectors see daughter of North Korea's Kim as heir apparent

SEOUL, South Korea — Until she fled North Korea three years ago, Kim Yumi felt deeply frustrated whenever state TV showed leader Kim Jong Un with his young daughter. The message, she felt, was clear and worrying: North Korea was laying the groundwork for an eventual hereditary transfer of power, this time to Kim's daughter.

Publicly questioning the Kim dynasty's hold on power would mean severe persecution. Already angered by draconian pandemic regulations that ruined her family's fishing business, she defected to South Korea by boat with her family.

"My husband and I didn't want our children to live under a fourth-generation dictatorship. As parents, we thought the best thing we could do for our children was to give them freedom," said Kim Yumi, 32, who now lives in Seoul.

North Korea allows no dissent and harshly punishes attempts to flee the country. Established in 1948, the nation is nominally a socialist republic, but in reality it is an authoritarian dynasty, with three generations of the Kim family ruling in succession. There was no known public resistance during its previous two successions — from state founder Kim Il Sung to his son Kim Jong Il in 1994 and then from Kim Jong Il to his son Kim Jong Un in 2011.

This time, North Korea is apparently trying something radical.

Kim Jong Un's repeated public appearances with his daughter over the past four years have led to speculation that she's being groomed as her father's heir.

The question of who will become North Korea's next leader is crucial because that person will face a huge challenge — governing an impoverished, nuclear-armed nation whose 26 million people have little political freedom and live under strict state surveillance while being cut off from much of the outside world.

North Koreans have no say in the selection of their future leader, and analysts and defectors say they will passively accept a third dynastic succession — at least publicly.

To gauge North Koreans' private views, The Associated Press spoke with nearly a dozen defectors who still have contacts in North Korea or witnessed the country's previous power successions, as well as several experts.

Most defectors believe the girl is Kim's heir

Not much is known about Kim's daughter except that she's reportedly about 13 and named Kim Ju Ae.

Since late 2022, she has made dozens of public appearances, all of them with her father at big events like weapons tests and military parades. State media has called her Kim's "most beloved" and "respected" child. Her status has been emphasized by images showing an elderly general kneeling before her and her standing in front of her father.

South Korea's spy agency says she is Kim's likely heir. Eight of the 11 defectors interviewed by the AP shared that view; the others disagreed, citing the North's deeply patriarchal culture.

"During her visits to missile launch sites and factories, the way senior North Korean officials treat Kim Ju Ae involves protocols reserved for a successor, not the ones simply for a daughter of Kim Jong Un," said Tae Yongho, a former minister at North Korea's Embassy in London who defected to South Korea in 2016. "They are repeating the same protocol and treatment they provided for Kim Jong Un," when he accompanied his father as his heir.

Kang Mi-Jin, a defector who runs a company analyzing North Korea's economy, said her contacts inside the North told her over smuggled phones that they think Kim Ju Ae is in line to succeed her father.

Jung Gwang-il, a defector who specializes in smuggling outside information to North Korea, said the North Koreans he meets as they visit Chinese border towns also hold the same belief.

Former NBA star Dennis Rodman was the first to reveal her identity, holding her as a baby during a 2013 trip to Pyongyang.

Doubts remain about a woman becoming North Korea's leader

Much of the skepticism about Kim Ju Ae as a potential leader stems from her being female. South Korean officials believe she has a younger sibling whose gender hasn't been confirmed.

Women in North Korea remain deeply underrepresented in senior posts. Only one of 17 department directors for the ruling Workers' Party is a woman. That woman is Kim Jong Un's influential younger sister, Kim Yo Jong, according to South Korea's Unification Ministry.

"My contacts in North Korea say it would be nonsensical to revere that little girl as their supreme leader," said Kim Jeong-Ah, a former North Korean army officer who resettled in South Korea in 2009.

Lee Si-young, a defector who heads the Seoul-based Free North Korea Radio station, said that some of her older contacts in North Korea aren't happy with a woman taking power. But she said members of the Kim family "are like gods reigning over humans so gender really doesn't matter."

Kim's push for hereditary power transfer faces little resistance at home

Whether or not the girl succeeds her father, observers agree that Kim Jong Un, 42, is likely to designate one of his children to prolong his family's rule, a move they expect would face little resistance at home. South Korea's spy agency recently assessed that Kim is extremely obese and at high risk of cardiovascular disease but shows no other signs of poor health.

North Koreans will passively "accept a hereditary succession as something that they should go along with," said Ahn Chan-il, a defector and scholar who heads the World Institute for North Korean Studies in Seoul.

During North Korea's first leadership transition, in 1994, the new leader, Kim Jong Il, then 52, had already spent two decades as the official successor working alongside his father to run the country.

The second succession, in 2011, was more uncertain. Kim Jong Un, who was then 27, was seen by outsiders as too young and inexperienced. He quickly consolidated his grip on power, however, by orchestrating high-profile executions and purges, including the 2013 killing of his powerful uncle Jang Song Thaek.

"A hereditary power succession system has been institutionalized in North Korea, just like presidential elections in our system," said Oh Gyeong-seob, an analyst at Seoul's Korea Institute for National Unification. "North Korea's ruling elite accepts it as a matter of course. So do its general citizens."

Choi Song-juk, who fled North Korea in 2015, said she had been so brainwashed that she had no complaints about the North's two earlier power successions. She now calls them "nonsense."

Defector Jeon Jae-hyun said North Korea's pervasive surveillance apparatus keeps people from voicing their discontent with the government and helps enforce political loyalty.

Defector Kim Yumi said she had never heard about the girl until Kim Jong Un publicly introduced his daughter at a long-range missile launch site in November 2022.

"Ordinary people know absolutely nothing about private lives of the Kim family," said Kim Yumi, who now runs a YouTube channel on North Korea. "They don't really try to know about it and don't pay attention to it because doing so could put them in danger."

entries.title: Indonesia's VP offers resignation as questions mount over his eligibility
entries.summary: His resignation offer comes amid a widening political rift between Prabowo and Widodo and a separate investigation into allegations that senior police officials wiretapped the president.
entries.content:
Indonesia's VP offers resignation as questions mount over his eligibility

JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesia's vice president offered to resign during a meeting with President Prabowo Subianto on Tuesday, according to officials, adding to the turmoil at the highest levels of the country's leadership.

Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko Widodo, held over two hours of talks with Prabowo, according to State Secretariat Minister Prasetyo Hadi.

It was not immediately clear whether Prabowo accepted the resignation, Hadi told reporters at a news conference at the presidential palace. The president advised Raka to "continue pursuing legal avenues to defend the validity of his academic documents," Hadi said.

As he left his office later in the day, Raka made a brief statement to reporters without addressing the resignation offer.

"I respect all criticism and feedback from the public regarding the developments that are taking place," Raka said. "I do not want the current situation to become a prolonged political controversy."

The resignation offer comes amid growing pressure on Raka over a court dispute involving his academic credentials. It was apparently not related to an ongoing probe into allegations that top police officials, including the president's chief of staff Gen. Listyo Sigit Prabowo, had been involved in a wiretap targeting the president. Three other police generals have also been implicated in the case.

Listyo previously served as national police chief under Widodo, who has not been implicated in the wiretapping investigation.

The developments come amid a widening political rift between Prabowo and Widodo. The popular former president backed Prabowo's presidential bid after he chose Raka as a running mate.

The controversy over Raka's academic qualifications escalated last month after the Supreme Court ruled that the documents he submitted regarding his overseas education did not meet election requirements.

The ruling intensified political pressure on Raka and fueled calls from some lawmakers for his impeachment.

Widodo faces unrelated allegations that he used a fake university diploma, which he denies.

entries.title: The average cost for a new vehicle in the U.S. hits a record high: over $51,000
entries.summary: Vehicle transaction prices are up to a new record high, according to the Kelley Blue Book — and some buyers are extending their car loans to finance them.
entries.content:
The average cost for a new vehicle in the U.S. hits a record high: over $51,000

Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.

The average transaction cost for a new vehicle has reached a record high: $51,109. That's according to a report out today from the Kelley Blue Book, which is part of the analytics firm Cox Automotive.

That's about $500 above the last record, set in December 2025.

Car prices have been stubbornly high for years, especially since the pandemic, mainly driven by supply chain issues. And they've gotten higher recently, in part thanks to tariffs and to buyers flocking to, and car companies making, larger, fancier vehicles.

Yet there's a little good news: Cars are getting more expensive … more slowly.

While that $51,109 figure is an all-time high, that's only up 2.1% in the past year.

"A 2.1% year-over-year increase is actually below inflation," said Erin Keating, an executive analyst at Cox Automotive who co-authored the report. Between 2012 and 2021, cars got 3.4% more expensive a year on average, she continued.

The Kelley Blue Book's transaction cost is based on what people wound up paying for a new vehicle — that means whatever's on the sticker price, plus add-ons for fancier features, and minus any incentives, such as dealer discounts.

It also doesn't include one other expense that adds to the cost of owning a car: interest on auto loans. The cost of borrowing has risen over the past several years as the Federal Reserve has kept interest rates high in an effort to drive down inflation. Auto loan rates are now about 11% for used vehicles and over 7% for new ones, according to Edmunds, a car analytics company.

Keating says all of this can add up to some sticker shock for buyers — partly because people don't buy cars all that often and can be surprised by how expensive they've gotten, and partly because of interest rates.

"I mean, we are seeing a true shift in the percentage of your monthly payment that's going towards interest versus towards principal," she said.

Used cars are not a steal

The Kelley Blue Book's average includes all kinds of vehicles — SUVs, pickup trucks, electric vehicles — from all kinds of auto companies, including Toyota, Subaru, Tesla and Mercedes-Benz.

It doesn't, however, include used car sales, which normally make up about two-thirds of total sales. Ivan Drury, director of industry insights at Edmunds, crunched those numbers too and found the same trend. "No matter what you're looking at, the price is up," he said.

The average used car now costs close to $27,000, 6% higher than last year, according to Cox Automotive. Vehicles that cost less than that are a "sliver" of the industry, Drury said.

Supply chain challenges, including a semiconductor shortage, during the COVID pandemic meant fewer cars got made. Carmakers had to pick and choose which vehicles to prioritize making — they picked their most profitable models. As a result, fewer used vehicles entered car lots in the early 2020s. So today there's less inventory to choose from.

That's good for people who already own a car, Drury said. It means people can upgrade to a new car without much additional money up front.

But, he continued, "The consumer that I sympathize with the absolute most? The first-time car buyer." Those buyers face a steep down payment, with nothing to trade in.

No matter whether buyers are choosing new or used, data from Edmunds shows that in 2026, they have been financing with lower down payments and longer auto term lengths. "We've just seen those explode," Drury said.

A report from Edmunds found that car buyers financed more than ever, taking out loans worth an average of $44,664 in the past quarter. They also found that more than a quarter of car buyers financed using loans with 84-month-long terms — or longer.

The combination of a small down payment — sometimes in the range of $500 or $1,000 — and a lengthy loan term can get really expensive for buyers in the long term, Drury said, especially with high interest rates.

"So people just say, 'Oh, forget it,' you know. 'I'll just, I'll just choose the longer term length and put less money down. I've got other bills that are pulling at me,'" Drury said.

Why are new cars so expensive?

In part, vehicles cost more because the cost of making them has gone up for automakers. There are now more tariffs on steel and aluminum, as well as on goods imported from Canada. That matters for American automakers who assemble vehicles on both sides of the border. The cost of computer chips (used in sensors and electronics) and copper (used for automotive wiring) has also risen thanks to competing demand from data centers.

But vehicles also cost more because Americans like bigger cars, SUVs and trucks, which tend to come with a higher price tag. The average sticker price for a full-size pickup truck is nearly $72,000, according to the Kelley Blue Book.

American carmakers have largely shifted their gears away from compact sedans. In earnings calls with investors, they've often cited American demand for bigger vehicles.

Plus, as analyst Mike Wall at Mobility Global points out, smaller vehicles offer lower margins for carmakers. "They were sort of that loss leader. It gets the eyeballs in the door," he said.

For the carmakers, they're not making as much money as they would compared to their bigger vehicles with pricier features.

Drury notes, people appreciate those features. They've gotten used to driving with 360-degree cameras, heated seats and parking assist systems. All of these drive up the cost of buying. "No one wants entry-level anymore," he said. "Everybody goes mid-to-upper trim levels."

"People love walking up to their car that already has the air conditioner going when it's 110 degrees outside, and think, 'You know what? I don't have to get in here and potentially burn my hands,'" Drury continued. "So as we get accustomed to more features, more options, we naturally kind of pile on, too. And automakers, they're very aware of that."

A challenging time for automakers

Over the past few years, "automakers have been under incredible stress," Keating said. Yes, there are tariffs and other rising production costs. Many also poured money into developing electric vehicle technology, but EVs still only make up a small slice of the U.S. car market. About 6% of new cars sold are electric, according to Edmunds.

And the market for car buyers is smaller. About 16 million people buy new cars every year — about 1 million fewer since the pandemic.

Notably, fewer people in their late 30s and early 40s are buying cars. "They're just simply holding onto their cars longer," Keating said. Her hypothesis? "That age group and that cohort is simply just dealing with different household pressures for their money and are making the choice to stay in the vehicles that they have."

For the most part, the people buying new cars tend to be older and wealthier. Keating said that might be because older drivers are staying on the road longer. " We have seen this interesting shift towards individuals keeping their licenses longer and therefore more 65 and up, 75 and up individuals are purchasing vehicles than ever before," she said.

For automakers, a drop in car buyers means they have to compete more with each other for sales.

"At the end of the day, each of these competitors are sharing, trying to go after a pie that isn't necessarily growing," Keating said. So instead, " they're stealing share from their competitors as opposed to counting on more consumers entering the picture."

entries.title: Seven days of chaos in the ER: How this country's healthcare system is unraveling
entries.summary: Renewed fighting has pushed Ethiopia's healthcare system close to collapse: "The whole emergency (room) was flooded with war trauma patients," one surgeon says of a brutal week in September.
entries.content:
Seven days of chaos in the ER: How this country's healthcare system is unraveling

In northern Ethiopia, conflict pushes a strained healthcare system to the brink

"It was a mess, it was chaos, and that continued for almost seven, eight days. Without (cell) network, without electricity," recalls a surgeon in Ethiopia.

On September 24, a two-year ceasefire between rebels and the Ethiopian government began to collapse. As injured people streamed in from the countryside, this surgeon and his colleagues treated as many as they could at a hospital in Mekele, the capital city of Ethiopia's northern Tigray region. Fearing repercussions for treating rebel fighters, the surgeon asked NPR not to publish his name.

"The whole emergency (room) was flooded with war trauma patients," he recalls. "The floors were all filled up, there was no place to step."

For the past several weeks, the violence has continued at a steady pace, raising concerns that Ethiopia could again face a civil war. The Ethiopian military has accused Sudan, Egypt and Eritrea of backing Tigrayan militants, who have aligned themselves with seven rebel groups in Ethiopia with the goal of ousting Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.

After drone strikes in late October killed at least 15 people, including children, the director-general of the World Health Organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, posted on X that the violence in northern Ethiopia "is pushing an already fragile health system closer to collapse."

During the initial outbreak of violence in September, the surgeon in Tigray says he spent days operating on victims of gunfire, drone attacks, and mortar shells. Some were clearly civilians, but others were fighters in uniform. Complicating matters, he recalls, there was no way to know how many patients were coming because cell service and the internet were cut.

"We don't know where they're from — you just go ahead and do whatever you can, you know?" he told NPR.

There had been signs that the war between Ethiopia's federal government and rebel groups could reopen. In May, Tigrayan rebels ousted regional leaders and installed their own. In response, Ethiopia's federal government cut funds to Tigray — including to hospitals run by the regional administration. Doctors, he says, haven't been paid in months.

"It's an open wound, which was never closed, you know. Left for healing and never healed," he says. "I guess now it's infected."

For Tedros of WHO, the situation is deeply personal. He is Tigrayan and previously served as Ethiopia's minister of health. In his social media post, he wrote that hospitals are facing shortages of workers, medicine and ambulances, and that WHO and the U.N. are working to deliver medical supplies to the affected regions.

"As fighting continues, more people are likely to lose access to essential healthcare … civilians must be protected," Tedros wrote. "The most courageous choose peace."

A worldwide worry

Public health experts say targeted attacks on healthcare —– generally considered a war crime —– have become a growing concern in conflict zones around the world.

So far in 2026, attacks on health care facilities and workers in 19 countries led to more than 960 deaths, according to data collected by WHO. While the largest mass casualty event occurred in a Pakistani airstrike on a drug rehabilitation center in Afghanistan, hundreds of people have died in attacks on healthcare settings in Sudan, Lebanon, and Ukraine.

Complicating matters are funding cuts to global health initiatives, including the dismantling of USAID shortly after Donald Trump took office in 2025.

"The continual attack against healthcare is eroding the norm of healthcare being a protected part of conflict," says Lindsey Green, a researcher focused on Ethiopia for the U.S. nonprofit Physicians for Human Rights.

The Tigray war lasted two years, killing an estimated 600,000 people. The majority of Tigray's health facilities were only partially functional, as the Ethiopian government imposed an aid blockade on the region — home to more than 7 million people.

Attacks continued, despite a peace agreement

The government struck a peace agreement with Tigrayan rebels in 2022, ending most hostilities, but attacks on healthcare continued. In August of this year, Physicians for Human Rights worked with the Organization for Justice and Accountability in the Horn of Africa to publish a report detailing these attacks.

Of more than 600 health workers surveyed across three regions of northern Ethiopia, 63% reported attacks on ambulances, some as they tried to reach injured patients, and 57% reported witnessing an armed takeover of their clinic or hospital between 2020 and 2024. One health worker in Mekele recalled Ethiopian forces occupying a hospital and placing the uniforms of Tigrayan rebels on the floor and forcing staff to step on them. "Nonsense stuff," he said.

"Armed groups were occupying facilities to take resources or to destroy resources, to destroy machines and equipment, really with the goal of making healthcare harder to access," Green says.

In the report, researchers confirmed targeted attacks on health care workers perpetrated by both rebels and government forces – often as retribution for a community's perceived alliances or against doctors who treated an enemy. But there has been no way for victims to seek justice from either party.

"It's very clear that this ongoing pattern of attacks on healthcare links back to impunity for these violations," Green says.

NPR reached out to Ethiopia's Foreign Ministry and Office of the Prime Minister, but did not receive a response.

Doctors in northern Ethiopia say the one-two punch of a war that specifically targeted healthcare, followed by foreign aid cuts, have left the region without a chance to recover.

A health worker in Tigray counted more than 100 women who died in childbirth over the past year. He attributed their deaths to the dire state of the health system. He spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity, due to fear of being targeted for speaking out.

"They died during delivery because of a lack of medicine, lack of health care providers, a lack of fuel. So the ambulances are not functional," he said.

An independent review of birth data during the Tigray war from 2020 - 2022 showed that the maternal mortality rate per 100,000 live births increased fivefold, compared to prewar data. Researchers in 2022 found that 83% of clinics and hospitals were no longer able to serve pregnant women. Additionally, systemic rape and sexual violence were regularly used as a weapon of war.

"They told us, the people should be punished, because we are supporters of the TPLF (Tigrayan rebels)," the health worker says.

Ayoda Werede, a California-based physician with the nonprofit, Health Professionals for Tigray, says that since the latest outbreak of violence, the Ethiopian military has not targeted health centers. But other unidentified groups have stolen supplies, "including medication, equipment, even mattresses off of patient's beds," Werede says. "This was just the opportunistic vacuum space that was created because of this conflict."

Her fear is that Ethiopia's healthcare system is already stretched beyond its capacity — and as the conflict reignites, injured people will have nowhere to go. The surgeon in Mekele has similar concerns. Many of Tigray's doctors, he says, have already left the country.

"We've lost our sense of being secure," he says. "It's a repeat of what's happened in the past."

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

entries.title: Get in, loser: Broadway's newest 'Mean Girls' are ready to insult (and enlighten) you
entries.summary: "School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play," is ending a Broadway run this week and celebrating with livestream broadcasts. We interviewed the Tony-nominated playwright, Jocelyn Bioh.
entries.content:
Get in, loser: Broadway's newest 'Mean Girls' are ready to insult (and enlighten) you

What would it mean to become Miss Ghana 1986? Fame, fortune, perhaps rubbing elbows with '80s superstar Bobby Brown? For a group of six teenage girls at the Aburi Girls Boarding School, the answer is: everything.

The battle for the crown is at the heart of School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play, written by Tony Award-nominated playwright Jocelyn Bioh. The play is ending a Broadway run this week and celebrating with livestream broadcasts on The League of Live Stream Theater's website for a fee (but is free for high schoolers).

School Girls is set at a boarding school in Ghana in 1986. It follows Paulina, the school's queen bee and her crew, whom she frequently belittles and bullies over their looks.

"So, do you want to be fat-fat? Or fit? And popular." Paulina asks Nana, harassing her over eating porridge instead of an apple at lunch.

Ahead of a visit from a pageant recruiter to the school, Paulina's plans to win Miss Ghana go awry after a new transfer student arrives: Ericka from … Ohio!

Ericka exposes Paulina's toxic behavior and shows her up during a performance of Whitney Houston's Greatest Love of All. Ericka, being lighter-skinned than Paulina, sparks a clash between the school's headmistress and the pageant director over beauty and who would have the best chance of winning the Miss Global Universe pageant.

Paulina becomes the victim of circumstances that she cannot control.

School Girls explores the themes of girlhood and impossible societal beauty standards with humor and humanity.

Although its title references the Tina Fey-penned 2004 film, Mean Girls, famous for its pink-hued portrayal of the toxic side of high school girls, Bioh says she wasn't actively thinking about the movie when writing School Girls.

After completing the play and needing to settle on a subtitle, Bioh found herself reflecting on the themes: "I'm like we're dealing with things and ideas and feelings and emotions." She said that her friend, actress Danai Gurira, described it as feral teenage girls. "I'm like, that archetype is incredibly universal."

A perspective on colorism

Beyond the talk about tiaras, '80s fashion and praise for Judy Bloom, School Girls tackles the issue of colorism head-on.

Bioh says she knew it was a topic she always wanted to write about after her own long journey to own her beauty as a dark-skinned woman. "I just wanted to write something that felt like it could maybe shorten the journey for somebody else who maybe felt the same way I did. Especially as a young, impressionable girl."

While School Girls approaches the topic from the perspective of Ghanaian women and girls, Bioh says the play's message has resonated with people from different backgrounds, underscoring that colorism is a global issue.

"'Cause who has decided that this one standard of beauty is the standard of beauty for everybody? I think that's a problem," Bioh explains. "I don't have a solution other than to, you know, create a play that people can feel entertained by or perhaps be impacted by, and hopefully shift their implicit bias as they move through the world."

The cast of School Girls displays a vast array of talent: Denée Benton (Paulina), Lucia Aremu (Ama), Nia Otchere-Sarfo (Gifty), Jordan Rice (Mercy), Erin Morton (Nana) and Jasmine Amy Rogers (Ericka), just to name a few. While it is an all-Black female cast, the diversity of physical appearance is clear.

"The audience, even if they are not young Black girls who went to school in Ghana, they still see facets of themselves in these girls. I think that's where the heart and beauty of it lies." Bioh says.

Audience reaction

School Girls is now on Broadway nearly 10 years after its Off-Broadway premiere. She says it's been a moving experience to see how the show's message continues to stay with audiences long after they leave the theater.

"I had a DM from Jenna Fischer of all people, who went to see the play a few days ago, and literally messaged me again today to say she's still thinking about the play," she says. "You know, how cool that someone who I just absolutely adore and also think is, like, a comedic genius, but who likely has never had any sort of experience with colorism, is still thinking about what the play is saying and how much it moved her.

For those who get to experience School Girls, Bioh hopes you have a good time and walk away with a deep sense of empathy not only for the young girls but for the adult women too.

"I ask people to shift their ideas about things," Bioh says. "If you can just move it just a little teeny bit, then I guess, you know, I've done my job."

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

entries.title: House set to vote to impeach Hegseth. And, SCOTUS allows border wall work to proceed
entries.summary: The House could vote to impeach Hegseth, but removing him from office will be tough. And, SCOTUS ruled that a federal judge did not have the authority to halt border wall construction.
entries.content:
Hegseth Impeachment Push, Trump Holds Off Iran Strikes, Congress Summons Nvidia's CEO

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

The House may vote this week on a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-KY, reintroduced articles of impeachment accusing Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanors. The eight specific charges include three charges for illegally waging war against Iran, one for ignoring laws to minimize civilian casualties, one for overseeing extrajudicial killings of alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific, and one for capturing Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro without congressional authorization. Hegseth has called the articles a sham.

  • 🎧 Only a few Republicans need to support impeachment in the House for it to be possible, NPR's Sam Gringlas tells Up First. This would lead to a Senate trial. Removing Hegseth from the Pentagon requires 67 senators, which will be challenging even once Democrats take control. But Massie told reporters he believes it will be possible, and opposition to the war in his fellow Republicans' home states could convince them to get on board. Massie says some members of Congress have come around to the idea that the administration must be held accountable for violating congressional war powers
  • ➡️ Also on House Republicans' agenda: a closed-door meeting today to pick a minority leader for the next Congress. The decision is down to current House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., and Ohio's Jim Jordan, a co-founder of the far-right House Freedom Caucus.

President Trump has acknowledged that the war he initiated with Iran harmed his party in the midterms. Weeks before the election, the president said he was going to hold off on any strikes in Iran. While campaigning, he hinted at potential actions to proceed with the war and teased a significant move to end it. Now, Trump says there's no need for further strikes if talks are ongoing.

  • 🎧 NPR's Deepa Shivaram says it's possible that Trump might resume military action if he doesn't get the deal he wants, because he has shown a pattern of shifting on his rhetoric since the war began. The president has also insisted that the war was necessary and he would do it again. Shivaram says Trump is starting to shift focus to shape his legacy in these last two years of his presidency. He is trying to frame the unpopular war as a success by saying Iran's nuclear stock is eliminated and that was his goal. In the remainder of his time in office, he wants to establish himself as a dealmaker and peacemaker.

Nvidia's stock slipped around 4.25% after CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence suspects of spying for China. This news sent shockwaves from Wall Street to Capitol Hill. AMD, Nvidia's main AI chip competitor, saw its shares jump more than 13%.

  • 🎧 Nvidia is central to the U.S.-China competition over AI, which could make Huang's statements and actions of high interest to Beijing, NPR's John Ruwitch says. The woman Huang admitted to having an affair with is an executive at MegaSpeed, a Singapore-based company that Nvidia has collaborated with. The controversy centers around whether MegaSpeed was helping Chinese firms bypass chip export controls. The New York Times reports that the U.S. Commerce Department is investigating MegaSpeed and that the woman was giving information to Beijing. NPR has not independently verified these claims.

The U.S. Supreme Court yesterday gave the Trump administration the green light to proceed with plans to build hundreds of miles of border barriers and security infrastructure in west Texas. The decision was made despite ongoing court hearings. This plan has faced bipartisan backlash for its involvement of Big Bend National Park, a cherished area known for its stunning canyons and pristine desert landscape. In a five-page decision, the Court asserted that the federal judge who issued an injunction against the construction lacked the authority to intervene.

Deep dive

Democrats did really well with Gen Z voters in last week's midterm election, snagging nearly a 50-point lead among voters under 30. This is a major comeback from 2024, when young voters leaned toward Trump. This year's results signal that the youngest generation of voters are issuing a strong rebuke of Republicans, and they're ready to fight for an American dream that feels just out of reach. Here's how Gen Z voters helped fuel a blue wave:

  • 🌊 Americans ages 18-29 have historically voted at lower rates than older voters. But this year, Gen Z accounted for 11% of the total vote. In the Texas Senate race, Democrat James Talarico won by 12 percentage points. Among Gen Z voters, he won by 60 points.
  • 🌊 Democrats credit their strong slate of candidates for boosting enthusiasm, but strong opposition to Trump also played a key role.
  • 🌊 Democrats gained support from some young voters who backed Trump two years ago, including white and Latino men. Both blocs voted blue by double digits this year. The party also narrowed the margins with young rural voters and those without college degrees.
  • 🌊 Some gains may have been influenced by young Trump voters who chose not to participate in this election, but it's unclear how many of them there were.

Picture show

Visitors, ecologists, park rangers and residents all cherish Cumberland Island, Ga., but they often disagree on the best ways to protect it. Feral horses, hogs and deer roam freely across the 18-mile island. Since 1972, Congress has mandated the preservation of thousands of wilderness acres under National Park Service protection. The island showcases a rich human history, including Native American artifacts, Spanish missions and grand Gilded Age mansions from the Carnegie era. Today, descendants of industrialist Thomas Carnegie still reside on private property. Now, a park service land-swap proposal with the family could greenlight new construction. The new development could ignite a clash among stakeholders over what true island preservation actually looks like.

3 things to know before you go

  • M. John Harrison's The End of Everything has won the 2026 Booker Prize. It follows Philip, who searches for "artifacts" along the coast of Kent, England, in a post-apocalyptic future.
  • British comedian Russell Brand has been sentenced to more than 10 years in prison after being found guilty on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
  • For his efforts to challenge menstrual stigma, 18-year-old Aadvik Jain is one of this year's recipients of the Diana Award, an international recognition for young changemakers working to improve lives in their communities.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

entries.title: Why did California's billionaire tax fail to surf the blue wave?
entries.summary: Two economists debate what California's vote on Prop 40 means for the wealth tax movement.
entries.content:
Why did California's billionaire tax fail to surf the blue wave?

Late Monday, The Associated Press determined that California voters had rejected Prop 40, the proposed billionaire wealth tax I wrote about last week. Given the big blue wave we saw during the midterms, why did this tax on billionaires fail to surf to victory?

To make sense of the results, I went back to the two economists I spoke with last week: UC Berkeley's Gabriel Zucman, a leading champion of wealth taxes, and Stanford's Joshua Rauh, a prominent critic of Prop 40.

Last week, they disagreed on what this wealth tax on billionaires would do to California's economy and tax revenue. Now comes the sequel, in which they disagree on what the results say about the politics of wealth taxes.

Their debate could foreshadow a bigger one in the next Democratic presidential primary: should the party embrace a wealth tax?

Did billionaire money tip the scales?

Zucman blames the corrosive influence of money for Prop 40's failure.

"I am not surprised," Zucman says. Opponents of Prop 40 spent almost $400 million fighting it, including spending on competing ballot measures, making it one of the most expensive ballot initiative fights in history.

"The money spent by the billionaires was critical," Zucman says. "Anyone who lives in California has been carpet-bombed by a deluge of ads. One can easily see how this could be pivotal in such a closely contested ballot."

But didn't Democrats win plenty of races this cycle despite huge sums spent against them? In Texas, for example, Elon Musk alone poured more than $150 million into defeating Democrat James Talarico. And Talarico ended up winning his Senate race by a comfortable margin. Why would money have been so decisive with Prop 40 and not in other races around the nation?

For one, Zucman says, the spending gap was much bigger in the fight over Prop 40. "The billionaires spent more than $300 million on ads versus negligible sums on the other side," Zucman says. "On TV and in their mailboxes, voters were exposed only to the anti-tax arguments. This was very different from the other midterm races: in those races, when spending was high (e.g., Talarico vs. Paxton in Texas) it was high on both sides, even if unevenly. The net difference in spending was considerably larger for Prop 40."

It's also possible that money can matter more in ballot initiatives than in races between candidates. Analysts have complained for decades that California's ballot initiative system is too easily manipulated by special interest groups. The nitty-gritty details of specific policies can get complicated, and many voters don't take the time to get educated on them. That can give well-funded advertising campaigns more power to shape their views.

In candidate races, meanwhile, voters can at least fall back on name recognition or party labels, which give them an easy mental shortcut — what social scientists call a "heuristic" — when making decisions at the ballot box. Even when they know little about the candidates, they usually know which party they prefer.

But Prop 40 didn't come with the same clear partisan signal. In fact, prominent Democrats, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom, came out against it. Newsom said he favored a national minimum tax on billionaires instead.

Or was this tax policy itself the problem?

"Popular opinion on wealth taxes is clearly not as strong as proponents thought," Rauh says.

Rauh questions whether money and advertising can really explain Prop 40's poor showing. He compared support for the tax with support for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. In some of "the most progressive Bay Area counties," he says, Harris won overwhelming support while Prop 40 won much less. This gap between support for Harris and support for Prop 40 was bigger there than it was in other Democratic-leaning counties across the state.

If advertising was the main explanation for this tax's poor showing, he argues, why was the gap so much bigger in the Bay Area? Sure, he says, advertisers may have done more targeting there, but he thinks the uneven pattern across the state casts doubt on the idea that advertising was the decisive factor.

"[T]he counties with the largest defections are actually the ones whose residents are most likely to know a billionaire, to work for one, or to have watched one move to Texas or Florida," Rauh writes in a recent post. "The simple reading is that proximity to the people being taxed, and to the businesses they fund, made voters more skeptical of the tax relative to their baseline politics."

For Rauh, that skepticism points to a broader conclusion: "The electorate even in progressive California has shown that it isn't ready for a wealth tax," he says.

More moderate Democratic voters, especially in affluent areas like the Bay Area, may simply dislike this novel way of taxing rich people in America and the consequences it could have. After all, this policy idea has divided Democrats before. During the 2020 presidential primary, Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders both championed wealth taxes, but rivals like Sen. Cory Booker and Michael Bloomberg opposed them. Joe Biden said he didn't oppose a wealth tax on the campaign trail, but early in his presidency, he declined to pursue Sen. Warren's wealth tax proposal.

Or maybe voters weren't rejecting the idea of a wealth tax per se. Maybe they were rejecting the particulars of this wealth tax.

For one thing, Prop 40 was a one-time tax, and it earmarked its projected revenue in ways that drew opposition from traditional Democratic allies. It allocated 90% of the revenue to health care, leaving only 10% for food assistance and education-related programs.

That helped put some typically left-leaning organizations in the opposition camp. For example, the California Teachers Association, a powerful teachers union. It argued that Prop 40 shortchanged public schools and did "not provide the sustainable and long-lasting funding that our schools and communities deserve."

Meanwhile, Prop 40 would have taxed billionaires at the state level. Supporters of a national approach argue that a wealth tax would be more effective at the national level because it's harder to leave America than it is to move to another state.

When Newsom came out against Prop 40 back in June, he wrote, "Wealth is movable, and it shops for the state with the lowest taxes. The fight belongs at the federal level, where this broken system was created in the first place."

Where does the wealth tax movement go from here?

Despite Prop 40's defeat, Zucman believes the wealth tax movement is far from over.

"With the blue wave nationally, the billionaire tax is going to be front and center in the new Congress," Zucman says. "Many of the newly elected Democratic senators have been campaigning on curbing the power and influence of billionaires. One can reasonably expect to see significant progress in the next two years."

Rauh also expects to see more wealth tax proposals in the coming Congress. But with President Trump in the White House, he sees little chance of one becoming law anytime soon.

"It will be the 2028 election that will really demonstrate the extent to which the public wants wealth taxation, as those proposals will likely feature prominently in political debate," Rauh says.

But even if wealth tax supporters win over voters, Rauh stresses they would encounter another big hurdle: the courts. He argues a federal wealth tax would constitute "a direct tax," a kind of tax that is subject to crippling constitutional restrictions.

As I explained in this 2019 Planet Money newsletter, the U.S. Constitution requires that "direct taxes" go through a complicated rigamarole in order to be constitutional. Specifically, the share of a direct tax's total revenue collected from each state has to match its share of the national population. That could mean wildly different tax rates depending on where people live.

This weird rule's history is tangled up with slavery. In one early Supreme Court case, one justice described it as basically a concession to Southern states seeking to limit federal taxation of their land and enslaved people.

The 16th Amendment exempted income taxes from this requirement. But that amendment doesn't mention wealth taxes.

Legal scholars disagree over whether this rule would doom a federal wealth tax. Is a wealth tax even a "direct tax"? That early Supreme Court case involved a tax on horse-drawn carriages that George Washington signed into law in 1794. The Court upheld it, a precedent wealth tax supporters point to today. For more on that story, listen to the Planet Money episode I did, "The Carriage Tax."

Stay tuned for more wealth tax coverage in the Planet Money newsletter in the future. We guess this movement isn't going away.

entries.title: U.S.-mediated talks on ending Russia-Ukraine war begin in Abu Dhabi
entries.summary: The two-day session in the UAE's capital, Abu Dhabi, is the first such meeting since February. It will focus on security guarantees, the White House said before the discussions.
entries.content:
U.S.-mediated talks on ending Russia-Ukraine war begin in Abu Dhabi

ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates — Three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States opened Tuesday in the United Arab Emirates, as Washington renews its push to end the war that followed Moscow's all-out invasion nearly five years ago.

The two-day session in the UAE's capital, Abu Dhabi, is the first such meeting since February. It will focus on security guarantees, the White House said before the discussions. Russia sees NATO as a threat, and Ukraine wants to prevent future Russian invasions.

Hopes of progress in ending Europe's biggest conflict since World War II are tempered by the absence of any significant breakthroughs in three previous rounds of talks early this year. The war has already killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians, analysts and humanitarian organizations say.

There are no signs the fighting is abating, and the talks took place against a backdrop of new long-range strikes between Russia and Ukraine. The two armies are largely deadlocked on the front line.

Russia launched 162 drones of various types and a ballistic missile at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine's air force said.

Meanwhile, Russia's Ministry of Defense said that its forces shot down 155 Ukrainian drones overnight above eight Russian regions, as well as the Crimean Peninsula, which Russia annexed from Ukraine in 2014.

Ukrainians meet first with European and NATO officials

U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, said on X that he and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff were working on a "negotiated solution that can deliver lasting peace and create the conditions for a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Ukraine within a more stable European security environment."

The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, noted at the start of the talks that the Russian delegation "has become bigger and more professional."

He expressed hope that the meeting "will allow us to advance on the path towards peace in the interests of the people of Russia and the people of Ukraine."

Rustem Umerov, the head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service who is leading Kyiv's delegation, said that the day began with a meeting between the Ukrainian team, the U.S. envoys and representatives from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission.

Russia and Ukraine hold to their divergent demands

The Russian and Ukrainian governments remain far apart on key elements of any prospective deal.

Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to pull its troops back from Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson — the four regions that Moscow annexed in September 2022 but never fully captured. He also demands that Ukraine abandon its bid to join NATO, accept strict limits on its military and drop restrictions on the Russian language and the Moscow-affiliated Orthodox Church in Ukraine.

Putin wants a comprehensive peace deal on those conditions and won't agree to a general halt in hostilities, arguing that it would only allow Ukrainian troops to rest and replenish their weapons stockpiles. He has warned that Russia will achieve its goals by force if Kyiv refuses to meet its conditions for peace.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who was visiting Denmark on Tuesday, rejects Putin's demands to voluntarily cede territory that Russia hasn't been able to take on the battlefield. Zelenskyy also rejects any limits on Ukraine's military or its arrangements with Western partners, which Kyiv sees as essential security guarantees to stop Moscow from invading again.

Ukraine argues that an immediate ceasefire is the necessary first step toward negotiating a wider settlement and says a direct meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy is the only way territorial issues can be settled.

Russia and Ukraine send experienced negotiators

The Russian and Ukrainian delegations include senior officials who have attended previous rounds of talks.

Russia's chief negotiator is Medinsky, a Putin aide who has led Moscow's team since the first direct peace talks with Ukraine in Istanbul in March 2022. The Russian delegation also includes deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov and deputy chief of the General Staff's operational department, Yuri Zhigarlovsky.

Apart from Umerov, the Ukrainian delegation also reportedly includes Zelenskyy's chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, his deputy, Sergiy Kyslytsya, and Davyd Arakhamia, the parliamentary faction leader of Zelenskyy's Servant of the People party.

U.S. says broader European security deal in the works

Last week, Trump declared that some kind of grand deal about European security was in the works, describing it as "a big agreement" that is "going to involve more than Ukraine."

Kushner said Monday on X that a "comprehensive and lasting settlement will also require direct engagement between Russia and our European partners on the broader security arrangements that affect them." The discussions in Abu Dhabi will set the stage for "that engagement to begin in the near future, as part of a broader multilateral process," he said.

Moscow has praised the broad approach.

"We can only welcome the (U.S.) negotiators on President Donald Trump's request proposing to put the issue of collective security on top of the agenda of the talks on a Ukrainian settlement," Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said.

Just before Moscow launched the full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, it demanded that NATO roll back its deployments in the trans-Atlantic alliance's member countries in Central and Eastern Europe, seeing their presence as a security threat. Similar demands will likely be part of any comprehensive peace deal proposed by Russia.

Kushner said that before the start of the three-way talks, he and Witkoff would meet separately with envoys from Ukraine, the European Union, NATO, Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Italy to "continue the close consultation and coordination we have undertaken on European security and Ukraine's postwar future over the past several weeks."

Some in the EU see Washington's proposals as too accommodating to Moscow.

Russia has objected to the Europeans' involvement in the three-way talks, but said that EU representatives could join at a later stage.

Russia and Ukraine have escalated aerial attacks

While the ground battles have morphed into a war of attrition along the 1,200-kilometer (about 750-mile) front line, Russia and Ukraine have ramped up their long-range strikes with drones and missiles.

Russia has intensified its air campaign against Ukraine's power grid, seeking to weaken the country's resolve as winter sets in. Moscow has relied on ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, taking advantage of Ukraine's shortage of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors.

Ukraine, meanwhile, has escalated its drone strikes on Russian oil refineries.

entries.title: House Republicans to elect a new leader as they look to rebuild from midterm defeat
entries.summary: After sweeping losses in the midterm elections, the House GOP will vote on Tuesday to elect a successor to Mike Johnson, who says he's stepping down as the chamber's top Republican.
entries.content:
House Republicans to elect a new leader as they look to rebuild from midterm defeat

Just one week after losing the majority in the midterm elections, House Republicans will meet behind closed doors on Tuesday to pick a minority leader for the next Congress.

The choice to succeed Mike Johnson, R-La., as the top House Republican will be between current House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., and Ohio Republican Jim Jordan, a co-founder of the ultra-conservative House Freedom Caucus.

The election — which will be conducted by secret ballot — represents a high-stakes decision for the party that will help determine which way it goes as it looks to regroup from a staggering defeat that saw Democrats flip more than 40 GOP seats en route to winning back the majority.

"I think what develops here will become a larger, external conversation about the direction of the Republican Party," said former House Speaker Pro Tempore Patrick McHenry, who held the gavel in an acting role during the tumultuous GOP speakership fight in 2023.

Republicans say they are ready to turn the page on their losses and start rebuilding to regain voters' trust. But first, they will have to decide between two candidates who would bring very different styles of leadership.

In Scalise, 61, House Republicans would be choosing a form of continuity — the No. 2 House Republican since 2023, and someone who has served in broader GOP leadership roles for more than 10 years. He's seen as more moderate than Jordan, and in a letter to colleagues announcing his candidacy, the close Trump ally said his approach to the job would be "conservative and consensus-driven."

"My number one goal as Republican Leader will be to win back the majority and I expect you to hold me accountable to that mission," Scalise wrote. "To succeed, we will need to be effective in both the oversight and legislative fights ahead, but we will also need to lay out a clear and optimistic vision for America."

"We have big tasks ahead, and tested leadership is needed now more than ever," he added.

In Jordan, 62, Republicans would be choosing a veteran of both the House Oversight and House Judiciary committees — two panels poised to play a central role in the new Congress as Democrats plan for a long list of investigations into President Trump and his administration.

A former college wrestling coach known for his pugilistic style, Jordan has pitched an aggressive posture to his colleagues, writing that "offense, not defense, wins elections."

"For too long, we have operated without a clear plan to survive the hour or the day in front of us. That will not cut it against an emboldened and energetic Democratic party," Jordan said in his letter to colleagues, taking a swipe at the House leadership team led by Johnson and Scalise.

"I am battle-tested on the oversight front and I know the Democrats' playbook," he added.

The contest is a rematch from 2023. Back then, Jordan and Scalise were vying to succeed Kevin McCarthy. After multiple candidates failed to secure enough votes, Republicans ultimately voted for Johnson.

Leslie Shedd, a Republican strategist, said the candidates will need to break through a process that can be like "family-on-family violence."

"It's really important … to lay out a very clear, substantive vision of how they plan to lead this conference out of what is now a desert," she said.

John Leganski, who was an aide to McCarthy, the former House Speaker, estimates more than 70% of the incoming House GOP conference was elected after Trump won his first term. As a result, they were largely made in his image or won because of it.

That means, Trump could wield a major influence over the direction of the House Republican conference as a result. So far, he's staying out of the race, though in 2023 he did endorse Jordan.

Leganski said that the size of Democrats' victory last week will limit leverage for Republicans under the eventual House Minority Leader when the new Congress is seated in January.

"I think whoever wins your job is to … number one, try to win back to the House," he said. "And number two, make life as difficult for the Democrats as possible, largely by voting no."

entries.title: How word of mouth is helping an Amish community's fight against measles
entries.summary: In Pennsylvania, health officials use a quiet vaccination campaign designed to win the trust of the state's Amish community, which has been hit hard by the measles outbreak.
entries.content:
How word of mouth is helping an Amish community's fight against measles

Measles spreads incredibly fast. For the last few months, so has Dale Weiser's phone number.

Weiser is the clinical services supervisor for the Chester County Health Department in south-central Pennsylvania. Since August, she's been driving out to Amish homes to vaccinate people against measles. She says it usually starts with a phone call.

"I was at a house, like, at 4:30 in the afternoon, and I had a phone call at 8 the next morning saying, 'hey, I heard you were down the street. Can you come do that at my house?'" she says of a typical request she gets from Amish families. So far, she's administered more than 400 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine in Amish homes.

The house calls are part of the state of Pennsylvania's strategy to wage war on measles by flipping the script on traditional public health messaging. Instead of advertising vaccinations loudly, health officials have launched a quiet word-of-mouth campaign designed to win the trust of the state's Amish community, which has been particularly hard hit by the country's worst measles outbreak in 35 years. The state has confirmed six measles-related deaths and more than 1,500 cases so far — though the true count is likely much higher, since many people who get sick don't seek medical care.

Lower vaccination rates

Surveys suggest only about a third of Amish families in the region vaccinate their children. That's left the Amish community especially vulnerable to measles, one of the most contagious diseases.

There's no religious edict against vaccination among the Amish. It's very much seen as a family and individual choice, says Weiser. Often, she says, these decisions are driven by practical and cultural factors.

"They don't have health insurance. They're not interacting with the mainstream medical society. And measles wasn't a problem for 30 years, so there was no real risk to not being vaccinated, at least for measles," Weiser says.

But as measles cases have piled up in Pennsylvania, Weiser says many Amish families have changed their minds about getting the MMR vaccine. And when they do, she hops in her car and brings the shots to them.

"When I arrive at their home, there's usually a small child that will run from the back of the house to the barn to tell the men that there's somebody strange in the driveway, or that the nurse is here," she says.

A patient, personalized approach to outreach

Some days, Weiser will vaccinate a single family in their kitchen. Other times, she'll find dozens of people gathered to get the shot. She's also fielded a lot of questions. Some, like what's in the vaccine and potential side effects, are things anyone would ask, she says.

"But I was caught off guard when I was asked if there were tracking chips in the vaccine, and I was like, whoa. Flashback to COVID. Where did you hear that?" she recalls.

Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

As with the general population, vaccine misinformation has made its way to the Amish community. And when she encounters it, Weiser takes the time to explain why the rumors are false.

Chester County Public Health Director Jeanne Franklin says this kind of patient, personalized approach has helped build trust among the local Amish – who, along with conservative Mennonites, are known as the Plain community because of their simple way of life.

"That's why we said it has to be boots on the ground in the communities. It's not just because they were a Plain community, it was because we needed to be seen as caring people," Franklin says.

Instead of relying on traditional top-down, rigid public health messaging, her staff has spent a lot of time quietly visiting Amish church leaders and businesses, introducing themselves and asking community leaders if they would hand out flyers advertising vaccine clinics. "One of them said, 'Come on back with a clinic' at his restaurant. And he helped spread the word," Franklin says.

Vaccine questions and misinformation

When I stopped by the restaurant, Honey Brook Barbecue in Honey Brook, Pa., an area with a sizable Amish community, I found the manager grilling chicken in an outdoor tent. Like many Amish people NPR talked to, he spoke on the condition of anonymity in keeping with his community's tradition of not drawing attention to oneself.

The manager says 24 people showed up to get vaccinated at his restaurant back in August, all drawn by word of mouth. He says he decided to host the clinic for two reasons: to protect the general public and to protect his own community. He said he didn't want people blaming the Amish for spreading measles.

But he says other people in the Amish community who don't regularly interact with the public aren't getting vaccinated. For some, it's because of cultural reasons, but he says others are concerned about what they've heard is in the MMR vaccine.

"In my community, a lot of it has to do with what people think is in it," the manager says of the MMR vaccine. One concern he's heard repeatedly is that the vaccine contains parts of aborted fetuses.

That is a myth often repeated by anti-vaccine forces, and it is one heard in conversations with Amish people in Lancaster County, home to around 45,000 Amish people. It's also the county with a third of the state's measles cases — more than 500 confirmed cases.

At the Amish-owned Gordonville Book Store, where a buggy is parked outside, I meet a shopper named Lydia Esh. She says she, her husband and six adult children had all previously been vaccinated against measles. But none of her 13 grandchildren have gotten the shot, because their parents had heard that the MMR vaccine had changed and now contained aborted fetus parts — which is false.

There is some evidence that anti-vaccine groups have been targeting the Amish in recent years, says Steve Nolt, a professor at Elizabethtown College who has written numerous books about Amish history and culture. For example, he points to an advertisement questioning the safety of childhood vaccines published in The Pennsylvania Busy Beaver, an advertising publication with a large Amish readership.

But in conversations around Lancaster, I also find evidence that public health outreach efforts are working. One member of the Plain community, a visibly pregnant woman outside an Amish-owned hardware store, says her husband and two children recently got vaccinated to protect her and her unborn child. She asked NPR not to use her name, as did an Amish man working at a produce stall in an Amish market. He says he recently got vaccinated because "measles is scary."

Linda Beth Fisher, an 18-year-old Amish woman behind the counter at the Gordonville Book Store, says she is concerned that several Amish people in her area have died in the measles outbreak, but she's not sure what to believe about the MMR vaccine.

"Personally, I'm kind of leery of it. I'm not sure why," Fisher says. "I guess I've just kind of heard that they're not good, but I've also heard that they are good. So I just feel like it's two sides of the story. Would you encourage people to get it?"

"They almost always come back"

These types of concerns often surface at pop-up vaccine clinics like one recently hosted at the Christiana Fire Company in Lancaster County. The Pennsylvania Department of Health hosts these events in Lancaster three or four times a week — all advertised by word of mouth, says Dr. Jennifer Wallace. As medical director for the department's Bureau of Community Health Systems, she oversees pop-up clinics and outreach to vulnerable communities across Pennsylvania.

Wallace says when members of the Plain community come with questions, "We're here to give them that information and then let them ponder it. They can ask any questions they want to and then let them either get vaccinated if they choose or take that information home. Think about it. Talk with their bishops. Talk with their community. They almost always come back."

Wallace says many who end up coming are families with multiple children. Tables set up around the firehouse are strewn with crayons, coloring books and bubble wands to keep young ones entertained while parents fill out paperwork.

"And then you see the kids get vaccinated and you can almost see the mother's shoulders relax over time as each child gets that shot," she says. "We've had some mothers cry afterwards because they're just so relieved."

The state health department says 30 people attended the Christiana firehouse clinic, 24 of whom got vaccinated. That included a father and his three sons who arrived for their second doses.
